messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos—a sixty-seven-year-old widower and a prosecutor for over thirty years—had spent his career in the controlled, predictable world of the courtroom, where rules and evidence governed every outcome. That world shattered one evening after a community outreach event, when a colleague he had trusted for years cornered him in an empty office. The man’s hand pressed against Carlos’s chest, the skin cold and damp, and Carlos felt a specific, sickening temperature on his own skin—a damp chill that seemed to seep into his bones even as the assault unfolded. He did not fight; he froze, his body a lead weight beneath the shock. In the weeks that followed, the memory of that touch would surface without warning, forcing itself into his mind while he was reviewing case files or standing in the courthouse hallway. The vividness was relentless: he could still feel the cold dampness on his chest, as if the man’s hand had left a permanent mark, and the memory often felt less like a recollection and more like something happening in the present moment, right there in the middle of his daily life.

The assault had left Carlos with a deep, corroding belief that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that even familiar faces could hide predators. Once he had concluded that the world was fundamentally dangerous, almost anything could confirm it—a door left ajar in the courthouse hallway, a colleague's unexpected approach from behind, the sound of footsteps in an empty corridor. He began to feel contaminated by what had happened, as though the cold touch had left a residue he could not wash off. His conviction that he was contaminated meant that ordinary encounters—a stranger standing too close in an elevator, a hand extended in greeting—now registered as potential triggers, each one carrying the threat of spreading the taint he felt inside. This sense of contamination made him avoid being around children—his own grandchildren, whom he had once adored—because he feared that his own tainted state might somehow transfer to them, or that their innocence would be shattered if he so much as looked at them. The belief that the world was dangerous also made him avoid unfamiliar places; he could not step into a new building without scanning for exits the moment he entered, his eyes darting to windows, stairwells, and doors before he could even register the room’s purpose. He noticed potential weapons everywhere—a letter opener on a desk, a heavy stapler, a glass paperweight—each object a reminder that danger could materialize in any setting. The more he scanned and noticed, the more the memory of the assault intruded, because each exit or weapon seemed to confirm that he was never safe. Already running on threat, he found that almost anything could tip into a warning—a janitor's cart left in the hallway, a door that was usually open now closed, a light flickering in the courthouse basement.

Over time, Carlos’s avoidance and hypervigilance began to reshape his life. He stopped attending the neighborhood association meetings he had once chaired, because the unfamiliar church basement where they met forced him to scan for exits for the entire two hours, leaving him exhausted and on edge. At work, he found himself avoiding the courthouse cafeteria because he could not sit with his back to the door, and he began eating lunch alone in his office. The belief that his body had been permanently damaged—a conviction that grew stronger each time the cold memory surfaced—made him avoid physical contact with anyone, even a handshake from a colleague. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found the courthouse had become dense with reminders he couldn't stop reading—the way a witness shifted in their seat, the click of a lock, the particular temperature of the air conditioning that sometimes matched that evening. He had come to believe that the assault had left him irrevocably changed, that his body was now a site of vulnerability and weakness. This belief fed back into his threat monitoring: when he scanned a room, he was not just looking for exits; he was also searching for anyone who might see his weakness and exploit it. The more he noticed weapons or dangerous objects, the more the memory of the assault forced itself into his mind, and the more he felt the cold dampness on his skin.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a moment in court. During a routine cross-examination, the defense attorney—a man Carlos had known for years—leaned forward, and the temperature in the room shifted. Carlos felt the same damp chill on his skin, and the memory surged unbidden: the cold hand, the empty office, the frozen silence. He lost his train of thought, stammered, and had to ask for a recess. He sat in the bathroom stall, his hands shaking, certain that everyone in the courtroom had seen his weakness. That night, he could not stop scanning his own bedroom for exits, and he found himself avoiding his own reflection in the mirror. He is most afraid that the contamination he feels will never leave him, that his body will always carry the mark of that cold touch, and that the world will always feel like a place where danger is hiding behind every familiar face. He is hoping that talking about it might make the memory feel less like a present horror and more like something that is truly over.
